title: CLAY COUNTY BOARD MEETS
full_story:
The Clay County Board met Tuesday evening.  Although there was a quorum in attendance, six members were absent.  Missing were Chairman Joe Goodman, Terry Woodrow, Rod Franklin, Terry Hronec, Jeremy Kohn and Cory Hodges.

In Joe Goodman’s absence, Vice Chair Barb McGrew took charge of the meeting.  After the agenda was approved, McGrew opened the floor to public comment.  Former board member Ted Whitehead briefly addressed the board.  He stated that if any board members needed to complete any required training, Snedeker Risk Management is conducting sexual harassment and cybersecurity training for the Village of Louisville and the Clay County Highway Department on October 1.  He encouraged them to attend and stay for lunch.

Next, Janice Brooks went over the Claims Committee Report.  It shows paid claims totaling $5,595,202 and unpaid claims of $684,623.  Members approved the report.

Jennifer Brown presented the 911 Report.  It shows all Telecommunicators received 100 percent for several months on their EMD quality assurance scores and are in high compliance with following the protocol standards.  The board learned that Magoo and Associates are considering different options for a different provider for backup internet.  And GTSI updated the 911 Board on the county-wide radio project with possible completion due in October.  Brown submitted two names to be re-appointed to the 911 Board for three-year terms from 2026 through September of 2029.  The board approved the re-appointment of Tim Hostettler and Todd Fender.

Clay County Hospital President/CEO Bob Sellers presented the Hospital Report.  He reported that concrete work at the hospital expansion and Clay County Health Department is making great strides and it won’t be long before walls will be going up.  He also asked the board to approve the purchase of a Cardiopulmonary PFT machine to replace the present unit that parts are no longer available.  The cost is $54,267.  The board approved the purchase.  Members also approved the Medical Staff Credentials for healthcare professionals.  Sellers also noted that the recent increase in Prevailing Wage Rates has resulted in an increase of $80,413 for the Hospital Maintenance Building and the board approved the change that now puts the cost at $749,628.  Sellers also noted that the state has restored grant funding they were expecting to the tune of $3.2 million.

Clay County Health Department Administrator Jeff Workman briefly went over highlights from the Board of Health Report.  He stated the Clay and Effingham County Health Departments are participating in the National Associations of Counties and Computer Aid, Inc. Cybersecurity Pilot program.  The Beyond the Bell program has equipped 22 youth with golf equipment and they are receiving training too.  Workman stated that it’s hoped students might earn golf scholarships in future years and could be a terrific option for students.  They are also working on robotics and STEM Programming.  In environmental health and emergency preparedness, health dept. staff have the opportunity today to remotely participate in the Illinois Vectorborne Disease Conference in Champaign.  Workman also noted that tick surveillance continues as does monitoring for West Nile Virus and they continue efforts concerning Cyclospora, immunization efforts for Measles and Flu Shots.  Workman closed by mentioning the continuing shortage of home care staff and noted that Brenda Young is retiring following a career that began at the health dept. in 1988.

Clay County Sheriff Andy Myers submitted his monthly report.  He also stated that a Greenville company is going to replace the center portion of the roof at the Clay County Courthouse.  He says it’s the last segment of the roof to be replaced.  It was installed 30 years ago in 1996.  The bid was $123,175.  But with an option to choose a thicker membrane and a 20-year warranty, the price was pushed to $125,340.  Members approved the bid unanimously.

In Circuit Clerk Crystal Ballard’s absence, Barb McGrew introduced a resolution that amends the establishment of Civil Fees and Criminal and Traffic Assessments to be Collected by the Clay County Clerk of the Circuit Court.  The measure was approved by the board without dissent.

Clay County Probation Officer Curtis Leib presented his report.  His report shows nine intakes for his department for August, with 271 active adult cases and 14 minors, putting the total caseload for his office at the end of August at 285.

Highway Engineer Darin Koelm presented a Bridge Aid Petition in Xenia Township for a culvert project on Palm Road and Honey Locust at a cost of $10,000.  Members approved his request.  In his Engineer’s Report he stated they are preparing for Fall and are wrapping up their mowing for the season.

In State’s Attorney Phillip Givens’ absence, Assistant State’s Attorney Cole Hilderbrand introduced information the state is requiring of counties.  He asked the board to Approve the Refund of the Tax Sale Purchase Amount to the Tax Buyer Pursuant to a Sale-in-Error.  The Principal Refund Shall be Paid from the Appropriate Collector’s Fund, and any Statutory Interest Due to the Refund Shall be Paid from the Tax Sale-in-Error Fund.  Following a brief discussion for clarification that included both Hilderbrand and Clay County Treasurer/Collector Stacey Allen, the board approved the measure unanimously.

Vice-Chair Barb McGrew was joined by Treasurer Allen for several successive measures all dealing with changes in Illinois law.  Members approved a resolution for the county to acquire all tax certificates and to appoint Clay County State’s Attorney to send delinquent parcel list to the County Treasurer.  They also approved a resolution for the creation of the surplus equity fund (a non-interest-bearing account).  They approved an ordinance to transfer surplus equity funds to corporate funds and pay all claims out of the Tort Liability Fund.  They also approved transferring Clay County Trustee Surplus Equity Funds from the Delinquent Tax Sale Auction Fund to the Surplus Equity Fund.

In other action, the board approved the replacement of a managed network switch in the amount of $2,035 to be paid out of capital expenditure funds.  Members also approved the purchase of six computer battery backup towers for the County Clerk’s office, in the amount of $1,457 to be paid out of capital expenditure funds.  The board also approved the replacement of the air conditioner at the Probation Office in the amount of $8,507 to be paid out of Capital Expenditure Funds.  However Sheriff Myers was quick to point out that this was a reimbursement.

The final action item of the night was the approval of the Hope Trust Health Insurance Renewal for county employees.  The monthly rate increase for employees for 2027 will be roughly 3 percent higher than the current monthly charge and the health reimbursement plan amount will increase by 5 percent.

title: FLORA CITY COUNCIL MEETS
full_story:
The Flora City Council met Tuesday afternoon, following the Labor Day Holiday on Monday.

Mayor Linda Spicer called the meeting to order and opened the floor to public comment. Flora resident Anthony Krutsinger appeared for the fourth time to ask the mayor and commissioners to stop using Flock cameras in the city. He said the cameras violate residents’ rights and asked how many people the council needs to see at meetings before they take action. He told the council there is no reason for the city to have the cameras and that he should not expect to be tracked every time he leaves his house. He suggested that sooner or later some people may take the cameras down themselves. He also asked if the council has heard from other residents besides him. Mayor Spicer was the only one to respond. She said she has heard some negative comments, but not all the comments are negative. After finishing his remarks, Krutsinger returned to his seat.

The mayor then asked the council to approve the meeting agenda and consent agenda, which they did without dissent. The consent agenda included past meeting minutes, the warrant list for the second half of August, and a request from the Clay County Farm Bureau to use Charley Brown Park on September 25 for Farm Safety Day, with a rain date of September 29. Members also set Trick or Treat night for October 29 from 6:00 to 8:00 p.m. They approved a request from Flora High School for the Homecoming Parade on September 23 and the associated road closures as submitted to the Flora Police.

In regular business, Mayor Spicer reminded everyone that the Flora Rotary Club’s Shadows of Elmwood Cemetery Tours take place this Friday and Saturday, starting at Flora’s historic B & O Railroad Depot. Tickets cost $8, and a benefactor ticket is available for $25 that allows holders to move to the front of the line for the next hay wagon. Mayor Spicer then sought to reappoint the Honorable Robin Todd and Jim Earleywine to five-year terms on the Zoning Board through September 8, 2031. The council approved both appointments unanimously.

The mayor then polled the commissioners for their comments. Commissioner Jeremy Henderson asked about the status of the downtown grants the city applied for. Mike Stanford told him he has made inquiries but has not yet heard back on those applications. Commissioner Phil Wiley echoed Mayor Spicer’s comments about the Rotary Club Cemetery Tours this Friday and Saturday from 5 to 9 p.m. He also reminded everyone that Ford Town is the following week and includes both a chili cookoff and a farmers market on that Saturday. Before ending his remarks, Wiley congratulated Flora Wolves Running Back Kormick Massie for setting the career touchdowns record. Massie scored three touchdowns Friday night at Dancey Field, raising the new mark to 40. The previous record stood for 80 years and belonged to standout Flora graduate Melvin Dold, who set it in 1946 and later became a two-sport athlete at Georgia Tech.

Next, Flora City Administrator and Economic Development Director Mike Stanford presented several items for the council’s consideration. In the absence of Lee Beckman of Milano and Grunloh Engineers, Stanford updated the board on the status of two grants. He said the ITEP sidewalk grants for Flora’s east side and the Industrial Park are still accepting letters of support from the community on the importance of installing the sidewalks for safety, and he encouraged people to submit photos showing people walking in those areas. The DCEO Grant for relining local sewers is also moving forward and remains important to the proposed wastewater treatment plant. That project would help filter out storm water rather than sending it into the sewer system. Stanford then asked commissioners to approve a resolution in support of the ITEP Grant for sidewalks on Vincennes Avenue and at the Flora Industrial Park. The council quickly approved it. Stanford then called on Matt Johnson with Fehr Graham Engineering and Environmental, who provided an update on the Wastewater Treatment Plant proposal. Johnson reviewed the proposal’s history from 2020, the various issues that arose from the original preliminary work, the period when progress stalled, the permitting problems, the termination of the person who had been leading Flora’s permit application, and the recent steps that put the project back on track. Johnson said the permit process is now proceeding and that officials believe construction can begin in the spring of 2027 with completion in 2028. With that news, Johnson explained that additional engineering services will cost $720,000. After he finished, Mike Stanford asked the council to approve an ordinance amending the city’s agreement with Fehr Graham Engineering and Environmental for that $720,000 amount. The measure passed 3-1, with Commissioner Jeremy Henderson voting against it. Commissioner Lacey Lewis was absent. Henderson had questioned whether the design is the best option for Flora. The overall cost of the Wastewater Treatment Plant is estimated at between $27.5 million and $33 million. Planning to replace Flora’s outdated plant originally began in 2016.

City Administrator Mike Stanford then asked the council to approve an ordinance authorizing the sale of real estate at 114 Park Avenue. It passed unanimously. Commissioners also approved an ordinance awarding the bid and sale of real estate at 717 N. State to Hickox Rentals, Inc., for $3,100. Stanford then announced two bid notices. The first is for remodeling the Flora Public Works Building, a budgeted project. The second is for the MFT Oil and Chip program for Flora streets, also a budgeted project.

To close the meeting, Flora City Treasurer Stephanie Bailey asked the council to approve the 2025 Motor Fuel Tax Compliance Review. The council approved it unanimously.

title: NEWMAN ARREST
full_story:
On May 7th, the Flora Police Department received a complaint regarding an adult male exchanging messages with a juvenile female.

Following an extensive investigation, an arrest warrant was issued on Friday, for Darrell J. Newman, 37, of Flora.

Newman was arrested later that same day on the warrant and transported to the Clay County Jail, where he is awaiting his first court appearance.

Newman faces 10 separate counts of Child Sexual Abuse Material.

The Flora Police Department was assisted in this investigation by the Coeur d’Alene Police Department, Idaho State Police, Wayne County Sheriff’s Department, and the Clay County State’s Attorney’s Office.

The Flora Police Department would like to remind the public that an arrest is not evidence of guilt.  All individuals are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.

title: XENIA VILLAGE BOARD
full_story:
The Xenia Village board of Trustees met in regular session last night.

Trustees were set to hear public comments from Todd Bradum and Brandon Bridges with Charleston Engineering.  Neither were able to attend. Mr. Bridges left a message with Xenia Village Secretary Melissa Eckhart.  Eckhart informed trustees that since they were opting not to resurface the section of road in the village owned by CSX railroad as part of the $1,075,000 road resurfacing project there would be 250 ft of asphalt the village would need to decide on a second location to resurface.  Trustees voted to repave the road in front of the villages community building.

Village trustees discussed rough sketches for the construction of a new village community building.  Trustees agreed the idea of a 120 x 50 ft pole barn style building would be the best option for the village and decided to move forward with commissioning official blue prints.  At this time there is no estaminet of cost or timeline for the construction of the project.  Trustee Ivan Barnett said, “at this point we have to do something the cost and up keep of the current community building is already pretty costly.”

Xenia Chief of Police Jerry Burkett told trustees everything was running smoothly in police business.

Melissa Eckhart on behalf of Village Superintendent Travis Lewis told trustees that oiling and chipping road work along Church to Cottonwood Street was completed and included the digging of a new culvert.

Trustees also discussed the upcoming elections.  Four trustee seats and the position of village mayor will be up for election.  A One hundred page handbook is available at Xenia Village community building for those interested in running for election.  Campaign forms will be available through October 19th and are due by October 26th.  A village caucus will be held December 7th.

The Xenia Village Fire Department Trick or Treat will be held October 24th from 5 – 8pm.  The Village will hold a ham and turkey bingo December 5th and is looking for sponsors.

title: CLAY COUNTY SHERIFF’S ACTIVITY REPORT
full_story:
Clay County Sheriff Andy Myers issued his monthly activity report during Tuesday’s Clay County Board meeting.  In the Report for August, the Sheriff’s Office issued a total of 23 Traffic Citations, made 24 Criminal Arrests and served 31 various Civil Papers.  A total of 22,412 miles were driven by Sheriff’s personnel during the month.

25 persons were processed through the Clay County Jail during August.  There were 6 inmates in jail at the beginning of the month and 4 in jail at the end of the month.  The average daily jail population was 6.

Also, the Clay County Sheriff’s Office received a total of $3,505 during the month.  This includes:

The Sheriff’s Office handled approximately 514 complaints, 103 of which originated in Louisville and 79 in Clay City.  The Sheriff’s Office conducted 35 Criminal Investigations and 10 Accident Investigations during August.

title: GEFF FRONTIER DAYS
full_story:
Geff Frontier Days will be held Saturday with more than 60 vendors expected to set up in the village park.  Organizer Julie Hall said there is an extraordinary vendor turnout offering crafts, food, antiques, farm products, homemade goods and other merchandise.

The Day begins with the Geff Ruritan breakfast at 7 am.  For children, Frog races begin at 9 am, followed by turtle races at 9:30 am.  A most-decorated baby contest and diaper derby will begin at 10 am, with a basketball shoot-out, sack and three-legged races, sawdust pile money hunt and pedal pull following throughout the day.

There will not be a Frontier Days parade this year, but the day’s schedule is packed with traditional events for children and adults to enjoy.  Frontier Days’ traditional ham and beans with cornbread will also be served beginning at 11:30 am in the Ruritan building, with the meal cooked over an open fire.  The quilt show will run from 8:30 am to 4 pm, with a quilting demonstration at the Town Hall at 10 am Car and tractor show registration begins at 9 am, and bingo starts at 2 pm.

Local entertainment is also planned throughout the day.  The Little Miss Geff Frontier Days Pageant for girls ages 6 to 9, will begin at 6 pm closing out the day.

Terry, Julie and Madeline Hall will be the guests today on the ReVue talking about Geff Frontier Days.

title: GRAIN BIN RESCUE
full_story:
A grain elevator employee trapped inside a grain bin was safely rescued using equipment purchased with an Illinois Farm Bureau Rural Development Grant.

At 10:21 am on August 27th, the Xenia Fire Department in Clay County responded to a report of a man stuck chest-deep in grain.  According to a release from the department, firefighters, with the assistance of local farmers, went to work right away, deploying a grain bin rescue tube to stabilize and protect the individual while waiting for mutual aid from the Clay County/Flora Rescue and the Marion County Grain Bin Task Force.

Once additional resources arrived, crews deployed grain bin rescue panels and other equipment, including augers.  Using a K-12 FD Rescue Saw, crews cut openings in the bin, removing grain to reduce pressure around the trapped worker.

“He was able to step up and out of the grain tubes and actually slid out the access hole himself,” said Xenia Fire Chief Vince King, noting they made at least three cuts with the rescue saw to remove enough grain.  “It was a huge sigh of relief and weight off our shoulders knowing we got him out.”

The fire department purchased the rescue saw, which allows firefighters to cut through metal buildings or objects, with funding from a 2024-25 Rural Development Grant awarded through Illinois Farm Bureau in partnership with county Farm Bureaus.  King said a smaller saw was brought to the scene as well, but was unable to cut through the grain bin, underscoring the value of the rescue saw.

“Programs like this help us be able to get this equipment into our hands that honestly would be out of reach for us with the current budget constraints,” King told FarmWeek.

Other equipment used by first responders, including the grain bin rescue tube, was also purchased with grant funding and donations available to rural fire departments.  King said “it’s just a godsend” that multiple funding opportunities exist to help departments obtain the equipment they need.

This rescue effort was one example of how IFB’s Rural Development Grants are benefiting communities and farmers.

Clay County Farm Bureau manager Hope Woodrow said grain bin accidents “hit close to home” for those in the agriculture industry.  She said she is grateful their community can help keep people safe and ensure they can come home to their families.

“Being able to be a part of a community that helps is incredible,” Woodrow said.

Reflecting on the impact of the Rural Development Grant the county received, Woodrow encouraged other rural communities to apply when applications open on October 1st.

“There are so many things that could help not only our emergency services but our communities,” she said.  “Receiving a grant could make an impact that saves a life.”
